entities.summary: Gaius Sulpicius Longus was a prominent Roman statesman and general of the late Republic, serving as Consul thrice and dictator once. He distinguished himself by leading the Roman army to victory over the Samnites in 343 BCE, a significant milestone in the Punic Wars. Longus's political career was marked by his ability to navigate the complex web of alliances and rivalries within the Roman Republic, earning him a reputation as a skilled diplomat and strategist. Despite his notable achievements, Longus's life was cut short when he died in 350 BCE, leaving behind a legacy that would be remembered for generations to come. His legacy can be seen in the many Roman laws and institutions that he helped establish, cementing his place as one of the most influential figures of the late Republic. The inscription on the Arch of Titus, erected in 82 CE, commemorates Longus's military victories, including his triumph over the Samnites.
